title: The world before Nanak
hook: his first var describes a dark age of empty ritual and quarrels over labels, before Nanak came

segments.voice: Yesterday, kunji, and your line, the key. Did you open a door for someone and then step aside? Today we use the key for the first time. Day six hundred ninety-nine.

Truth, left standing on the bank, while two men quarrel themselves to ruin. That's one of the pictures Bhai Gurdas paints in his first var, before Guru Nanak has even been born into the story. Before the hero walks on, a storyteller shows what's wrong with the world he walks into. Bhai Gurdas spends a good stretch of his first var doing exactly that, and he doesn't go easy. Today: kalyug.
screen: `TRUTH, LEFT ON THE BANK.` → `SETTING THE STAGE.` → `THE WORLD BEFORE NANAK.`

segments.voice: Bhai Gurdas calls it the kalyug, the dark age. And look at what he says is dark. Not a lack of religion. There's plenty of religion in his picture. People divided into castes on one side and into rival schools on the other. Hindus heading for the Ganges and Banaras, Muslims for Mecca and the Kaaba. One side proud of the sacred thread and the forehead mark, the other of its own outward signs. Both call on God, Ram for some, Rahim for others, and Bhai Gurdas says it's one Name, but they lose their way on two roads. Pride, stubbornness and quarreling fill the space where devotion should be. And then the line from the hook: truth stood off on the bank while the Brahmin and the maulvi wore each other out. Hear this carefully, because it's easy to mishear. Bhai Gurdas isn't attacking Hindus, or Muslims, or their scriptures. In the same passage he says people forgot what their own books taught. His target is what happens when a label, a mark or a place of pilgrimage becomes the whole of faith, and the people under the labels stop seeing each other. He is painting a mood in the world, not grading anyone's religion. That's the darkness: ritual with nobody home, and neighbors turned rivals over names for the same God. Then, at the end of the stretch, the turn. Bhai Gurdas says the generous Lord heard the cry of the world, and sent Guru Nanak into it. The stage is set. The light comes tomorrow.
screen: `THE KALYUG: A DARK AGE.` · `PLENTY OF RELIGION, LITTLE TRUTH.` · `ONE NAME, TWO ROADS, ONE QUARREL.` · `THE CRY IS HEARD.` · then, large: `BEFORE THE LIGHT.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: notice one empty ritual in your own life. Not a religious one, necessarily. A habit you go through with nobody home. Saying "fine" when someone asks how you are. Scrolling the same three apps before you get out of bed. A thank you you say without looking up. Find just one. Don't scold yourself for it. Just sit with it for the length of the bell and ask what it was once meant to be for. If you pray, you can ask for that one thing to be filled again. The bell holds the time.
Kalyug, the dark age Bhai Gurdas pictures in his first var: labels, quarrels and empty ritual, with truth left standing on the bank, until the cry was heard.
Your line: before the light. Today, take the one empty ritual you found and do it once with someone home: say how you really are, or look up for the thank you. Day six hundred ninety-nine.

howItsDone: Sikhs reading Bhai Gurdas's first var hear its opening stanzas as the backdrop to Guru Nanak's coming: a world where outward signs and rivalries had crowded out devotion to the one Name.

myth: Bhai Gurdas says the dark age had no religion in it
it had plenty: pilgrimages, marks and rival schools, with truth left on the bank.
Bhai Gurdas aims his complaint at one community
he names Hindus and Muslims alike; his target is empty ritual and the quarrel.
the dark stretch ends with the cry of the world being heard
the generous Lord hears it and sends Guru Nanak.

fork.setup: you're a poet about to tell the life of Guru Nanak. before he arrives, how do you describe the world?
options: a golden age that only needed polishing.
a dark age, full of religion, quarreling over labels.
a world that had never heard of God.
fork.reveal: Bhai Gurdas paints a world crowded with pilgrimages, marks and rival schools, where people called on one Name and lost their way on two roads.

trapdoor: what you thought: the world before Nanak was a world without faith.
what it means: in Bhai Gurdas's picture, faith had shrunk to labels, places and marks, and people fought over them.
what a scholar hears: he names Hindus and Muslims side by side, in matching lines, so the darkness belongs to no single community.

sources.ref: Vaaran Bhai Gurdas, Var 1, pauri 21 (four castes, four schools; truth left on the bank)
Vaaran Bhai Gurdas, Var 1, pauri 23 (the cry heard; Guru Nanak sent)

notes: Var 1 pauri 21 paraphrased from memory (chaar varan chaar mazhabaan... sach kinaarai reh gaiaa khahi marde baahman maulaane). Confirm the pauri number and that the paraphrase is close: castes and schools, Ganges/Banaras and Mecca/Kaaba, thread and mark, Ram and Rahim one Name on two roads, forgetting their books, truth left on the bank.
Var 1 pauri 23 (suni pukaar daataar prabh, Guru Nanak jag maahi pathaaiaa) paraphrased. Confirm the number.

Sensitive framing: the script says plainly that Bhai Gurdas is not attacking Hindus, Muslims or their scriptures. Confirm a Keeper is comfortable with this reading, and that Hindu and Muslim listeners would feel fairly treated.
The circumcision line in the pauri is rendered as 'its own outward signs' to keep the description general. Confirm.

Editor: hook no longer invents 'fight in the water' (the pauri says Brahmin and maulvi quarrel to death while truth stays on the bank); 'riverbank' made 'bank'; cut the stock 'every good storyteller' line.
